definition: So good that it serves as a model for others to follow.
example: Her exemplary attendance record earned her a certificate at the end of the school year.
nuance: Exemplary means worth copying, not just very good; excellent praises quality without suggesting that others should imitate it.
prompt: A community center is choosing which volunteer to honor at its annual dinner.
options: The committee honored Jonah's exemplary service and urged others to follow his lead.
The committee honored Jonah for his exemplary service, though he missed nearly every shift.
Jonah was exemplary from volunteering this year because his schedule was full.
Jonah's exemplary rudeness to visitors embarrassed the entire committee.
reasons: Work that others are encouraged to imitate is exactly what deserves this praise.
Skipping most shifts sets a poor model, so the praise contradicts the facts.
This confuses the word with exempt, which means freed from a duty.
The word carries strong approval, so it cannot describe a fault that embarrasses people.

practice.prompt: A soccer coach reflects on how a player behaved during a tense championship game.
options: The coach drew an exemplary of a perfect pass on the whiteboard for the team.
Her exemplary sulking on the bench dragged down the whole team's mood.
The coach held up her exemplary sportsmanship as a standard for younger players.
Her exemplary sportsmanship led the referee to eject her for arguing every call.
reasons: The word is an adjective, not a noun; the writer means example.
Sulking is a flaw, and the word is kept for behavior that deserves admiration.
Conduct a coach presents as a pattern for others is what the word describes.
Being thrown out for arguing is misconduct, not behavior anyone should copy.
